Maladaptive Strategies.value: try hard not think about the trauma
Going out at night or being outside after dark
Any form of physical contact with others

Memory.value: I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it
When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event.
Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory

vignette: Kofi had always been drawn to a career in law enforcement, but nothing could have prepared him for the trauma he experienced during his first year as a detective. He was 18 when he was kidnapped by a suspect he had been investigating, held captive for three days in a cramped, dingy room with no windows. The only sounds were the muffled voices of his captors and the creaking of the old building. Kofi's mind racing with thoughts of escape, but his body was frozen in fear. When he was finally rescued, Kofi thought he had put the ordeal behind him. But as time passed, he began to notice that certain things triggered memories of those three days. The sound of footsteps outside his apartment at night would send his heart racing, and he would lie awake, convinced that someone was coming for him again. He started avoiding going out at night, opting instead to stay indoors, where it felt safer. Kofi also found himself recoiling from physical contact with others. A touch on the arm or a pat on the back would make him flinch, transporting him back to the feeling of being restrained and helpless. His girlfriend, Nia, noticed the change in him and tried to be understanding, but Kofi couldn't explain why he felt this way. He just knew that it made him feel vulnerable. When memories of his captivity did surface, Kofi struggled to put them into words. He would try to describe what happened, but the words wouldn't come. It was as if his brain had locked away the details, and he couldn't access them. But the sounds were still there, echoing in his mind - the creaks and groans of the old building, the muffled voices of his captors. Sometimes, Kofi would feel a wave of fear wash over him without any clear memory or image to explain it. It was as if his body remembered the trauma even when his mind didn't. He would be in the middle of a conversation with Nia or working on a case, and suddenly he would feel like he was back in that cramped room, fighting for air. As the months passed, Kofi's avoidance behaviors started to take a toll on his relationships and his work. His colleagues noticed that he was distant and preoccupied, and his performance began to suffer. Nia felt like she was losing him, like he was disappearing into himself. Kofi knew he needed help, but he didn't know where to start. One night, as he lay awake listening to the sounds outside his apartment, Kofi realized that he couldn't keep living like this. He needed to confront what had happened and find a way to heal. The thought of facing his memories head-on terrified him, but it also gave him a glimmer of hope. Maybe, just maybe, he could learn to live with what had happened and find a way to move forward. The next morning, Kofi made an appointment with a therapist, taking the first tentative step towards recovery. As he sat in the waiting room, he felt a sense of trepidation mixed with determination. He knew it wouldn't be easy, but he was ready to face whatever lay ahead, one small step at a time.
